main.title: The Game Awards
main.subtitle: A shared archive of the work we remember
main.summary: A celebration of game makers, with every category winner from 2014 onward.

cards.heading: What the awards celebrate
cards.text: The Game Awards celebrates the people who make games: designers, artists, writers, performers, composers and the teams around them. Created by Geoff Keighley in 2014, the annual show combines awards with performances, announcements and conversations about the medium.

cards.heading: A changing medium, a shared stage
cards.text: An awards archive is also a record of changing priorities. Categories make room for new ways to play and new kinds of work, from independent production and performance to accessibility and community support. Move through the years to read every category winner, then open the official ceremony beside the list.

main.title: Crisis Core: Final Fantasy VII Reunion
main.subtitle: Knowing the ending does not exhaust the journey
main.summary: On December 13, 2022, Square Enix released Crisis Core: Final Fantasy VII Reunion on PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch and PC.

cards.heading: Knowing the ending does not exhaust the journey
cards.text: Square Enix released Crisis Core: Final Fantasy VII Reunion for PlayStation, Xbox, Switch and PC on December 13, 2022. It updates the 2007 PSP prequel about Zack Fair with rebuilt models, revised environments, fully voiced dialogue, new musical arrangements and faster combat. The original missions, story and Digital Mind Wave remain central to the adventure.

cards.heading: Updating combat without replacing its core
cards.text: Zack's attacks respond more quickly, ability selection is clearer and transitions between action, magic and commands are smoother. Encounters still centre on one protagonist, with the Digital Mind Wave producing effects during battle. Changes to timing and presentation make that established framework easier to use on contemporary controls.

cards.heading: The Digital Mind Wave turns memory into a mechanic
cards.text: The Digital Mind Wave cycles reels and character images during combat. Their results provide effects and power-ups while recalling Zack's relationships. The player continues fighting as these outcomes emerge, so the system combines direct action with a degree of unpredictability. Reunion preserves this unusual part of the PSP game's combat.

cards.heading: An audiovisual reconstruction must reveal its era
cards.text: Rebuilt models and revised environments give the original scenes a new presentation. Fully voiced dialogue and rearranged music update their sound as well. The missions and direction retain the structure of the PSP adventure, letting its older pace coexist with more recent graphics, lighting and audio.

main.title: Preserving play
main.subtitle: Keeping the decisions, not only the executable
main.summary: A playable game, a prototype and a remembered development story preserve different kinds of evidence.

cards.heading: More than the image on the screen
cards.text: A game is more than its final image. Controls, timing, hardware, distribution and the people around it shape the experience. Preserving one version is valuable, but it does not automatically preserve every way the game was played.

cards.heading: A creation made explorable
cards.text: Digital Eclipse's Gold Master Series places games beside documents, prototypes and interviews. Its 2023 opening title, The Making of Karateka, lets the audience trace a creation rather than only receive a verdict about its importance.

cards.heading: Different ways to preserve play
cards.text: Museums and community projects also preserve source code, packaging and oral histories. Emulation and restoration help maintain access to software as original equipment ages. Each approach answers a different question, and the most useful collections explain what survives and what remains uncertain.

cards.heading: A collection with more to discover
cards.text: Pixel Museum is a curated starting collection, not an exhaustive history. Follow the sources, look at the objects closely and make connections between rooms. The medium's history is still being written by the people who make, play and preserve it.

features.title: A city in a small file
features.summary: Immersion makes its materials with code.

cards.heading: A file contains the instructions
cards.text: Ctrl-Alt-Test's Windows PC intro Immersion depicts a city rising from the sea, rendered in real time as a non-interactive presentation. It belongs to the 64k intro category, whose executable must fit into a very small file. Algorithms generate the materials for its pictures and sound as the program runs. A video capture records one performance; the executable contains the instructions that produce it. The size limit makes code, graphics and music depend on one another throughout production.

cards.heading: A deadline changes the finished work
cards.text: The group traces its idea to a conversation after watching competitors at Revision 2015. They hoped to return with something comparable, missed the following year's deadline, and released a version in 2017. Their postmortem acknowledges that the second half was unfinished. Work continued before the final version appeared that December. The story concerns tools and taste as well as file size: an image of a submerged city gave the team something to build towards, while a competition deadline exposed the distance between that intention and its implementation.

cards.heading: A work made for an audience
cards.text: The Finnish demoscene's living-heritage submission describes people collaborating on code, graphics and music, then showing the results at parties. Competitions make those roles visible to an audience, often through public voting. It names Assembly, which began as a demo party in Helsinki in 1992, alongside smaller gatherings. These occasions help explain why making the executable is only part of the activity. A work also needs an opportunity to run, other people to watch it, and a community able to discuss what it is doing.

cards.heading: Keeping the practice accessible
cards.text: Demoscene productions circulated on floppy disks, through modem connections and later over the internet. Participants also preserved files and the knowledge needed to run them, with museums taking an increasing interest in their work. Tools, machines and presentation conditions can all affect what an audience sees. Preserving a production therefore involves maintaining its executable alongside information about how it was made and shown, while gatherings give experienced practitioners a place to pass on those skills.

features.title: Counting games outside the shop
features.summary: A market snapshot needs a date.

cards.heading: Give the headline a date
cards.text: Phil Salvador and the Video Game History Foundation turned a familiar frustration into a research question: how many older games could people still obtain commercially? With the Software Preservation Network, they examined a random sample of 1,500 games released in the United States before 2010. Volunteers checked availability and the team reviewed their results. The July 2023 explanation reported only thirteen percent in release. Its evidence was dated through April 15, 2023, giving the headline a particular market and a definite moment in time.

cards.heading: Which version counts?
cards.text: The team's decisions about editions mattered. An enhanced Jinxter kept the underlying text adventure and counted as available, while Yakuza Kiwami's reconstruction did not make the original Yakuza available under the study's test. Salvador explained these judgments alongside the results. The question concerned a reasonably accessible release, not whether somebody still owned a surviving copy. Games could remain on shelves in private collections or archives while disappearing from the marketplace. Counting commercial access made that gap visible beyond the familiar bestsellers still being sold.

cards.heading: A shop needs continued work
cards.text: Two years earlier, a publisher had shown how quickly an announced boundary could move. On April 19, 2021, Sony's Jim Ryan reversed plans to end PlayStation Store purchasing on PS3 and PS Vita that summer. He described the original decision as a response to the difficulty of supporting commerce on older devices and the desire to concentrate resources on newer ones. Continuing a shop required work behind the familiar menu. The decision concerned the infrastructure through which players could still buy games.

cards.heading: Players change a decision
cards.text: Ryan also acknowledged the players who wanted those older shops to remain. His announcement credited their response and said Sony had found a way to continue operations. PSP commerce still had a stated retirement date of July 2, 2021, so the reversal drew a boundary between platforms. Read beside a later availability survey, the episode gives the numbers a human setting: players argued for access, a company reconsidered its priorities, and the means of buying older games changed through a dated decision.

features.title: Repair keeps play within reach
features.summary: Different futures call for different repairs.

cards.heading: Tuesday evenings in the workshop
cards.text: Tuesday evenings gave the PDP-1 restoration a rhythm. Mike Cheponis remembered the Computer History Museum's volunteers meeting from six until nine, with a firm promise to leave by ten however tempting the next experiment. A whiteboard held their checklist. Joe Fredrick led hardware work, Eric Smith led software work, and Al Kossow gathered documentation and tapes. Behind the return of Spacewar! stood a practical arrangement for people giving their evenings to a machine: shared tasks, recorded progress and a time to stop.

cards.heading: Leave a trail of changes
cards.text: Cheponis described a repair that left a trail. Removed components were kept with dates, locations and reasons for replacement; new parts received identifying red marks. The team discussed difficult decisions together and could consult curator Dag Spicer. Even the existing contents of memory were copied before more extensive use. Returning the machine to service meant deciding what evidence to retain along the way. The project treated a successful demonstration and a documented account of its changes as parts of the same job.

cards.heading: Thirty-six computers return
cards.text: At Britain's National Museum of Computing, the destination was a classroom. A 2015 Fix-A-Beeb day brought twenty volunteers together to repair stored BBC Micros for students and visitors. Organiser Owen Grover reported that failed power supplies were the most common problem. The museum expected about twenty restored machines; the group rebooted thirty-six before exhausting the available spare components. Those computers would replace failing classroom units, keeping old machines available for people learning BASIC or returning to games they remembered from school.

cards.heading: A classroom changes the brief
cards.text: Some donated BBC Micros carried their owners' improvements. Extra ROMs and external connections for speakers or headphones showed how people had adapted the machines. Grover said the repair group removed such additions to improve reliability for classroom use. That decision gave the computers a different future from the individually customised lives they had arrived with. A working teaching collection needed dependable replacements ready for the next group of visitors. The work joined component repair to a choice about how the repaired object would be used.
